scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for a parent to force their 13-year-old son to play sports or join an extracurricular activity. The parent is really frustrated because the son is lazy, doesn't do well in school, doesn't take care of himself, and seems to have no work ethic. The parent's ex-partner isn't helping, so they're taking the initiative to try to change their son's habits.

First, I need to consider the parent's intentions. They're not trying to live out their own sports dreams through their son; they genuinely want to help him develop a better work ethic and get out of his comfort zone. That seems positive. They're thinking of starting with a season of basketball, giving the son a chance to try it out and see if it works for him. If he doesn't like it, he can quit after the season. That shows some flexibility and consideration for the son's feelings.

On the other hand, forcing the son into an activity he might not want to do could have negative consequences. It might lead to resentment or resistance, especially since the son is already showing a pattern of not wanting to do anything unless he has to. The parent is worried about the son becoming a "loser," but forcing him into sports might not address the root issues, like his laziness or lack of motivation.

I should also think about the alternatives. Are there other ways to encourage the son without forcing him? Maybe setting up a reward system for completing tasks, or finding an activity that the son is actually interested in. It's important to involve the son in the decision-making process so he feels some ownership over his choices.

Another consideration is the parent's own behavior. They're taking action because the other parent isn't, but it's important to model the behavior they want to see. If the parent is frustrated and pushing too hard, that might not be the best example for the son.

In terms of morality, forcing someone into an activity can be seen as controlling or disrespectful of their autonomy. However, as a parent, there's a balance between guiding and forcing. The parent's intention is good, but the method might not be the most effective or respectful.

So, weighing the intentions against the methods, it's a bit of a gray area. The parent is trying to help, but forcing might not be the best approach. It could lead to negative outcomes, so maybe it's not morally acceptable.
